title: Verifier‑Grounded Evaluation of LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: A Preregistered NetConfig‑Semantic Study
abstract: We present a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1; preregistration SHA‑256 7db1663cf3982c8ea1e16c3dd7c0348f356bb4cbe3978ecc75bb59fdedb71a37) that compares a deterministic template baseline to a single‑pass LLM generator (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini) on N = 120 synthetic intent→configuration tasks using a deterministic validator. Under the frozen confirmatory semantics (shared_initial_candidate per pair) the deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) produced identical verdicts for both conditions: baseline = 120/120 verifier passes; guarded (gpt‑5‑mini, seed_0) = 120/120 verifier passes. The paired difference is 0.00 (95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0). We (i) publish the exact execution and analysis artifacts and SHA‑256 fingerprints needed to reproduce the run, (ii) diagnose—using archived artifacts—why the paired outcome is uninformative about independent generative reliability (preregistered shared_initial_candidate design, template‑tight task synthesis, and validator–task coupling), and (iii) provide artifact‑grounded, runnable modifications (independent_per_condition sampling, multi‑seed confirmatory design, validator diversity, expanded task heterogeneity) that preserve reproducibility while producing informative independent comparisons. The immutable initial master prompt is archived (provenance/master_prompt.txt; SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba).

sections.introduction: Modern NetOps increasingly seeks high‑level intent→configuration automation that is safe, correct, and auditable. Large language models (LLMs) are a promising route to natural‑language intent translation, yet their stochastic generation and propensity for semantic errors complicate operational trust. Deterministic configuration verifiers (e.g., Batfish‑class tools) compute semantic effects (reachability, ACL invariants, transient safety during multi‑step changes) and are used in practice to prevent misconfigurations [10.1145/3603269.3604866]. This work asks a concrete, preregistered question: can a reproducible benchmark using deterministic template baselines and an open‑source verifier reliably detect and quantify semantic errors (reachability, ACL equivalence, BGP policy preservation) in LLM‑generated device configurations across vendor syntaxes and topology classes? We preregistered CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1 to answer a narrowly defined confirmatory estimand: the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline across N = 120 programmatically synthesized tasks under a frozen shared_candidate generation semantics. All design elements—task generator, seeds, validator, scoring rule, and stopping policy—were frozen before model calls (preregistration SHA‑256 7db1663cf3…). The run and all artifacts are published to permit exact byte‑for‑byte reproduction.
sections.related_work: Two literature strands are most relevant. First, deterministic network configuration verification and pre‑deployment analyzers (Batfish and successors) provide computational oracles for reachability, ACL semantics, and transient safety; lessons from Batfish’s industrial evolution emphasize the importance of high‑fidelity parsers and scalable semantic engines [10.1145/3603269.3604866]. Second, recent LLM→NetOps work investigates intent translation, generate–validate–repair loops, and guarded agentic architectures; these studies repeatedly highlight that token/fluency metrics fail to capture operational correctness and that verifier grounding is essential for trustworthy automation (examples include CNSM 2024 work on LLM configuration generation [10.23919/cnsm62983.2024.10814407] and a comprehensive survey of intent‑based configurations with LLMs [10.1002/nem.70029]). Our contribution is methodological: a frozen, preregistered paired design with deterministic validator traces, exhaustive SHA‑256 artifact manifests, and a published deterministic reconciliation enabling exact reruns and artifact‑anchored diagnosis.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The preregistered study CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1 (SHA‑256 7db1663cf3...) specified: (i) N = 120 tasks (40 per topology class: edge, datacenter, multi‑AS); (ii) confirmatory paired design with primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; (iii) generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" (one canonical candidate per task shared across conditions); (iv) deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version 5.0) implementing full_intent_constraint_validation as the binary pass criterion; (v) stopping rules and retry policy (up to 2 automatic retries for infrastructure failures). The frozen preregistration and execution manifest are in the artifact bundle (see execution/execution_manifest.json). The exact initial master prompt used to drive autonomous steps is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba).

Task generation and templates. Tasks were synthesized deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (version 5.0). Each task manifest entry encodes: initial_state, expected_final_state, explicit required_sequence (the exact per‑field operations that must be executed safely), workflow_policies (e.g., make‑before‑break, minimum_active_in_groups), and allowed_touched_fields. Representative task manifests and canonical candidate responses are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; representative examples in artifact_examples). The templated design ensures each task has an unambiguous validator‑checkable required_sequence; this is operationally realistic for many carefully specified maintenance workflows but narrows distributional diversity relative to open natural‑language intents.

Generation semantics, adapter, and model. The declared model used in the run is gpt‑5‑mini accessed through provider adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the pinned model configuration is archived at execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics, for each task a single canonical candidate (shared initial) was generated and stored under execution/responses/*-shared-initial.txt; that canonical candidate was re‑evaluated by the validator in both baseline and guarded episodes to isolate downstream scoring differences. Provider call traces and the call cache are archived under execution/provider_calls/ and execution/call_cache/ for exposure auditing.

Deterministic validator and scoring. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 parses candidates, normalizes command order, enforces per‑task workflow_policies (including transient safety invariants), and computes final_state reachability and ACL invariants. The scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation returns a binary score: VALID_CONFIGURATION (1) if the candidate satisfies all required_commands and transient constraints, else 0. Each scoring episode emits a JSON trace with parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, and final_state (execution/scoring/*.json). Representative scoring JSONs (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 0d56c1add7c5a57f...) include before/after validator states and violation lists.

Confirmatory analysis plan. The analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 computes per‑task binary success under baseline and guarded episodes, forms the paired contingency table (n_11,n_10,n_01,n_00), reports mean paired difference, bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), and exact McNemar two‑sided p‑value. Missingness and failed‑call policies follow the preregistration: infrastructure call failures would trigger retry; none occurred in this run. All analysis artifacts (condition_summary.csv, paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis_log.jsonl) are archived under analysis/ with SHA‑256 fingerprints.
sections.results:
Execution accounting (artifact‑grounded). The run completed in scientific_confirmatory mode with planned_episode_count = 240 (120 task pairs × 2 conditions). Execution manifest records completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 120 (shared_initial generation counted once per pair), and full artifact manifests and per‑file SHA‑256s are available under execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/*. See execution/execution_manifest.json and the many per‑file hashes included in the bundle for exact byte‑level reproducibility.

Primary confirmatory outcomes (artifact‑grounded counts). Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the deterministic validator produced identical pass outcomes for baseline and guarded: baseline_success_count = 120/120 (pass rate = 1.00); guarded_success_count = 120/120 (pass rate = 1.00). The paired contingency table is degenerate (n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0), stored as analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (SHA‑256 9f25790c...). The mean paired difference = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) is [0.00, 0.00]; the exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All analysis files, plots, and logs are archived in analysis/ (paired_difference_figure.svg SHA‑256 ae5b8e0c...).

Representative episode traces. To illustrate the artifact grounding, we call out three representative artifacts included in the bundle: (1) execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 8f38c8becd7e1e36...) contains the canonical candidate for task‑000001; (2) execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (SHA‑256 0d56c1add7c5a57f...) is the validator trace showing parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, normalized_configuration, and violation_count = 0; (3) execution/task_manifest.jsonl contains the task payload for task‑000001 including required_sequence and workflow_policies (see artifact_examples). Across many pairs the baseline, guarded, and shared‑initial response files are byte‑identical (identical SHA‑256), which directly explains the identical scoring outcomes.

Contamination checks and exposure. Preregistered contamination heuristics (exact match and normalized n‑gram overlap) were applied to confirmatory candidates; analysis/contamination_summary.csv records no flags under the pre‑specified thresholds. The run publishes all provider calls and call_cache entries (execution/provider_calls/*.json and execution/call_cache/*.json) so independent auditors can reapply exposure tests with alternative thresholds; absence of a contamination flag is not proof of zero exposure to pretraining corpora, which we note as a limitation.

Deterministic reconciliation. The deterministic_reconciliation.json artifact confirms internal accounting consistency: complete_pair_count = 120, baseline_success_count = 120, guarded_success_count = 120, model_calls_used = 120, cache_miss_count = 120, and all deterministic consistency checks passed (artifact hash analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json). This file is published to permit exact verification of bookkeeping claims.
sections.discussion:
Why the confirmatory test is degenerate. The archived artifacts show causality: preregistered generation_semantics = 'shared_initial_candidate' produced a single canonical candidate per task and reused it for both baseline and guarded scoring episodes (see execution/responses/*-shared-initial.txt). Given a deterministic validator and template‑aligned candidate that satisfies the required_sequence, both conditions necessarily receive identical pass judgments. Thus the confirmatory paired test measured whether the validator's scoring differed across conditions for an identical artifact (it did not), not whether independent LLM generative reliability differs from the deterministic template baseline.

Operational interpretation. For NetOps deployment decisions, the metric of interest is usually the per‑condition independent pass probability of the generator ("If I sample a fresh output from the model, what is the probability it will pass the validator?"). The preregistered shared_candidate design intentionally disabled this source of variance to isolate scoring differences; the artifact‑grounded result (0.00 paired difference) is therefore arithmetically correct but substantively uninformative about independent reliability. The published artifacts enable researchers to rerun the same deterministic validator with independent_per_condition generation semantics or with multi‑seed replication to estimate independent pass probabilities while preserving exact reproducibility (the same task manifests, seeds, validator code, and scoring harness are provided).

Recommended artifact‑grounded remediations. Using the included bundle, three runnable modifications produce informative inference about independent generative reliability: (A) independent_per_condition confirmatory sampling—generate independent candidates per condition per task (e.g., seed_0 baseline, seed_1 guarded) and re‑run deterministic_netops_validator_v5; (B) multi‑seed confirmatory replication—generate K ≥ 3 independent seeds per condition per task and compute per‑condition pass probability with bootstrapped paired contrasts; (C) validator diversification—add a second independent verifier (e.g., an emulator or alternate semantic analyzer) and report intersection/union pass rates to mitigate validator–task coupling. All fixture paths and validator invocation scripts are included so these reruns can be executed deterministically.

Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded). Internal validity: the preregistered shared_candidate semantics removed generation variability and thus prevented the confirmatory test from probing independent generation reliability; this is documented by identical response SHA‑256s across baseline/guarded pairs (execution/responses/*). Construct validity: the deterministic validator enforces task templates’ required_sequences, potentially over‑rewarding candidates that align with template structure relative to open natural‑language intents. External validity: this run tests a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini as recorded in execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2...) on synthetic templated tasks, limiting generalization to other models and broader natural intent distributions. Conclusion validity: the degenerate contingency table leads to trivial inferential statistics that are correct but do not address the operational question of independent generative robustness. These limitations are explicitly captured in analysis/missingness_summary.csv and deterministic_reconciliation.json.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, verifier‑grounded paired experiment and released a complete artifact bundle enabling exact reproduction (execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/*). Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics both the deterministic template baseline and the gpt‑5‑mini guarded condition validated on all N = 120 tasks (both 120/120). Archived evidence—shared initial candidate files and validator scoring traces—shows that identical canonical candidates per pair and template‑tight tasks caused the degenerate paired outcome; consequently the confirmatory paired result does not provide evidence about independent LLM generative reliability in operational settings. We provide artifact‑grounded, runnable modifications (independent_per_condition sampling, multi‑seed confirmatory execution, validator diversification, and task heterogeneity expansion) that preserve reproducibility and enable informative independent comparisons. All execution and analysis artifacts—including the immutable master prompt reference (provenance/master_prompt.txt; SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) and the preregistration SHA‑256—are included in the submission bundle to permit exact audit and follow‑up experiments. Transparent preregistration plus exhaustive artifact publication clarifies exactly what a confirmatory test measures and accelerates corrective reruns that answer practitioners’ operational questions about LLM reliability in NetOps deployments.

limitations: Controlled synthetic tasks: programmatic templates produced narrow required_sequences and workflow_policies that favour canonical solutions and limit external generalizability to heterogeneous operational intents.

Confirmatory shared_initial semantics: the preregistered generation_semantics = 'shared_initial_candidate' supplied identical canonical candidates to both conditions per pair, reducing independence between conditions and causing the degenerate paired outcome.

Single canonical seed for confirmatory test: the primary analysis used one canonical seed per task; preregistered exploratory multi‑seed analyses (seeds_1..4) were not included in the confirmatory inference reported here.

Validator–task coupling: the deterministic validator enforces constraints encoded in the task templates, which can increase pass rates for template‑aligned candidates and reduce construct validity for open distributions.

Possible training‑data exposure: preregistered contamination heuristics found no flags under chosen thresholds, but absence of a flag is not proof of zero exposure to related artifacts in model pretraining.

Single‑model, single‑validator run: results apply only to gpt‑5‑mini under the recorded configuration and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; they do not generalize across model families, agentic pipelines, or other validators.
